conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your cardiac surgery team doctors. You’re here today for your coronary artery bypass surgery. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nervous, but okay. I’ve been having more trouble walking without getting short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re doing this. Your heart isn’t getting enough blood through two major arteries, and this bypass will help improve that. You’ve already had all the tests, and everything looks ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under general anesthesia. The surgery takes a few hours. We’ll use your internal mammary artery and a vein from your leg to create three new pathways around the blocked areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? I know they’ve been weak since last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. Your baseline creatinine is 1.5, and we’ll avoid anything that could stress your kidneys. Nephrology is on board if we need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just updating you — you’re in the recovery area now. The surgery went well. You’ve had a triple bypass: one artery from your chest and two vein grafts to your heart. You’re on a breathing machine for now, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just reviewed your chest X-ray. The breathing tube is in a good spot, but we’ll adjust it slightly. Your lungs look clear, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back. Your breathing has gotten a little faster, so we checked another X-ray. There’s mild fluid in the lungs — common after surgery. We’ll watch it closely and adjust your fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I feel a little tight in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. Your heart is adjusting after surgery, and we’re giving you just the right amount of fluid. It should improve in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re off the breathing machine now. You were extubated this morning and breathing on your own. How’s your breathing feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still weak, but I can breathe. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started a beta-blocker and a diuretic to help your heart work efficiently and reduce fluid. We’ll also remove the Swan-Ganz catheter and put in a central line for medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray confirms the new central line is in place. Your lungs still have some atelectasis — collapsed areas — but that’s common. We’ll keep encouraging deep breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest tubes were removed this morning. That’s a big step. You’re healing well, and your breathing is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little better. But my legs are swelling a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some swelling is expected. We’re watching your kidney function closely because your creatinine went up to 3.1. That means your kidneys aren’t filtering as well right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Last time it caused problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s acute on chronic kidney injury — we expected this risk. Nephrology is involved, and we’ve paused the diuretic for now. The good news is your urine output is good, and your weight is slowly coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray shows your heart is a bit enlarged, but no change in fluid. We’re not concerned about tamponade. Your lungs still have some atelectasis, but it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for pulmonary edema. The latest X-ray shows improvement in lung fluid, which is excellent. Your heart is adjusting well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cardiac silhouette is slightly larger, but you’re not showing signs of tamponade. We’ll keep monitoring. If anything changes, we’ll do an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a burning when I pee. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be a urinary tract infection. We’ll test your urine. With the catheter, UTIs can happen after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test came back — you have Pseudomonas, a type of bacteria. It’s sensitive to ciprofloxacin, so we’re starting that antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not if we treat it. Pseudomonas can be tough, but cipro will work. You should feel better in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous. Vomited once last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray. It was hard to see, but there’s no sign of a blockage. Nausea can happen after surgery, especially with antibiotics. We’ll give something for nausea and keep you hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news — your creatinine is stable at 2.9, and your infection is responding. You’re making real progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go to rehab soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ll go to extended care rehab. You’re still weak and need help moving, but your wounds are healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes? My sugars have been okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose has been under good control. You’ve only needed insulin occasionally. As you eat more, we’ll watch closely. If sugars go above 140 often, we’ll adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on clopidogrel, amlodipine, metoprolol, and rosuvastatin. We’re switching from nebivolol to metoprolol because it’s safer with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I’m allergic to aspirin. Is that still an issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you’re on clopidogrel instead — it’s similar and safe for you. No aspirin. We’ll keep that on your chart clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my legs? They still hurt from the vein harvest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The incisions are healing well — no redness or drainage. You can use tramadol for pain. Keep them clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my chest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sternum is healing well. No signs of infection. Wear a supportive bra to reduce pulling. No lifting over 10 pounds for 10 weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t be able to drive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for about a month. Wait until your follow-up with the surgeon. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help at rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll need two people to help you move for now. Your goal is to walk with a cane again. You’ve had a stroke before, so rehab will focus on strength and balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What labs will I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Twice weekly blood tests for kidney function — BUN, creatinine, and potassium. The results go straight to nephrology. We’ll follow up with cardiology and surgery too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my kidney get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect it will improve over time. It’s a combination of your chronic condition and the stress of surgery. Staying hydrated and avoiding certain meds will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel more at ease now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. Your labs are stable, infection is treated, and your heart is doing well. We’re discharging you to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Nervous, but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Remember: shower daily, check your incisions, weigh yourself every morning, and take your temperature at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No creams on the cuts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct — no lotions or powders. Just mild soap and water. And call us if you see redness, drainage, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve been through a lot, and you’re on the mend. Rehab will help you regain strength. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last X-ray before discharge — shows your heart size is stable, no fluid in lungs. Everything looks good for transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go. Just want to keep getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. Keep up the deep breathing, stay active as you can, and follow the rehab team’s guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot — what about the heparin shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get heparin injections three times a day to prevent clots. The rehab nurses will give them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool softener?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Docusate twice a day, and polyethylene glycol daily. We don’t want constipation — it can strain your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re well prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little sad to leave — you all have taken such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. This is just the next step. You’ve had a major surgery, and you’re healing well. We’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — incisions clean, breathing good, vitals stable. You’re cleared for transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep getting stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll miss you all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll miss you too. But this is a good goodbye — you’re on the road to recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re proud of you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels to rehab. We’ll be checking in.
